**Vatsal Maurya, Joy M. Monteiro, Anish Sugathan, Deepak Malghan**

**Status:** Under review.

## Overview

High-resolution climate-health analyses often aggregate meteorological inputs, composite heat metrics, or threshold exceedances across space and time. Because these operations are nonlinear, changing the order of aggregation and transformation can change the answer.

The project uses Jensen's inequality as a framework for quantifying these discrepancies in the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) and associated heat-stress exceedance calculations.

## Key results

- Jensen gaps are systematic rather than random.
- Their magnitude and direction depend on the heat-stress threshold being used.
- The biases are spatially clustered.
- Bias introduced during heat-metric construction and bias introduced during threshold exceedance do not combine additively.
- At high thresholds, district averaging can report no exceedance even when individual grid cells within the district experience heat-stress exceedances.

## Method and results from the thesis defence

The three slides below are reproduced **unchanged** from my BS-MS thesis defence. The text beneath each slide is only a guide to what to look for.

### 1. The aggregation problem

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-method.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-method.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide explaining the Jensen gap in UTCI and threshold-exceedance calculations."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> the Jensen-aware route computes UTCI or threshold exceedance at every hourly grid point and aggregates afterwards, whereas the convenience-aggregation route averages meteorological inputs first and then applies the nonlinear transformation. Because UTCI is neither globally convex nor concave over most of its domain, the sign and magnitude of the gap must be established empirically.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 2. The bias is spatially structured and threshold-dependent

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-results-spatial.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-results-spatial.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide showing district-level heat-stress exceedance and spatial Jensen gaps across India."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> the exposure maps and corresponding Jensen-gap maps show that aggregation bias is not random in space. Its direction also depends on the UTCI threshold: the same district can be overestimated at one threshold and underestimated at another.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 3. Aggregation can change which districts appear most at risk

<figure class="research-figure">
<a href="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-results-ranking.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/jensen-slide-results-ranking.png" alt="Original thesis-defence slide showing changes in district heat-stress rankings under Jensen-biased aggregation."></a>
<figcaption><strong>What to look for:</strong> reducing the analysis to ordinal rankings does not remove the problem. District rankings can shift substantially under the aggregated calculation; in the defence results, the largest illustrated change occurs for Mayurbhanj at the 46 °C threshold.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The normative choice inside aggregation

Aggregation is not only a computational convenience. Choosing a spatial scale, temporal scale, or exceedance threshold determines which forms of exposure remain visible after data are compressed.

That makes these choices relevant to questions such as **whose exposure is represented by a district average, which vulnerable populations can disappear inside an aggregate, and what threshold a heat-action plan should treat as harmful**. The quantitative framework is therefore also a way to make the consequences of those normative choices explicit.

## Why it matters

Administrative heat planning operates at aggregated scales, while heat exposure occurs locally. The project shows why the scale and order at which environmental data are processed can affect policy-facing conclusions.
